title: A Dynamic Murmur / HCM Means Risk Assessment, Not a Blanket Sports Ban

blocks.text: A Dynamic Murmur / HCM Means Risk Assessment, Not a Blanket Sports Ban

Code R5-120 · Physical examination · PACES Station 3, cardiovascular examination · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10 minutes (up to 6 examining; at least 4 questioning) · UK hospital outpatient setting · Source dates listed in §15 · AMaC examiner-style educational station; not an official PACES marking scheme.
Please examine this patient’s cardiovascular system to establish a possible cause of their cardiac murmur. Present your findings and answer the examiners’ questions.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. A dynamic systolic murmur and jerky pulse suggest obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The clinical task is to recognise possible obstruction and discuss risk, family screening and sport without false certainty.

The Examiner Trap. The candidate labels every systolic murmur aortic stenosis, or automatically bans all sport. Pass behaviour is to identify dynamic obstruction and request specialist, individualised exercise and sudden-death risk assessment.

blocks.text: Not applicable — this is an examination encounter with a patient, not a communication or consultation role-player. The patient may answer brief, natural questions but is not a surrogate.
Patient setup: A 32-year-old recreational runner, stable, diagnosed with a thickened heart muscle during family investigations.
Finding-release protocol: do not announce a sign before the corresponding manoeuvre is performed.
The patient is comfortable at rest; normal peripheral perfusion and no oedema.
A brisk, jerky carotid pulse; double apical impulse; an ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge that increases with standing and decreases with squatting.
No basal crackles, raised JVP or signs of decompensation.
Normal-findings variant: If no murmur is audible today, report the normal auscultation explicitly and continue the HCM risk assessment from the history and available records.
Examiner question ladder (4–6 questions; 4-minute discussion):
Q1 [R2]: What diagnosis best fits?  Model: Likely hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with dynamic LV outflow obstruction; echo confirms morphology and gradient.
Q2 [R3]: What changes the risk discussion?  Model: Unexplained syncope, family premature sudden death, ventricular arrhythmia, ventricular structure and CMR findings.
Q3 [R4]: What will you offer the family?  Model: First-degree relatives need clinical screening and appropriate genetic counselling or cascade testing.
Q4 [R5]: Can the patient run?  Model: Not a universal ban; specialist shared decision after risk assessment, tailored to symptoms and the sport.
Q5 [R6]: When might mavacamten be used?  Model: In eligible adults with symptomatic obstructive HCM despite individually optimised standard care under NICE TA913.

Curveball: The candidate states a diagnosis with certainty before discussing alternatives. Safe response: “These are findings and a leading differential; confirmation needs the appropriate investigation.”
[R1; Skill A] Examine pulse, apex, murmur with posture and heart-failure signs.
[R2; Skill B] Describe a jerky pulse, double apex and dynamic systolic murmur.
[R3; Skill D] Identify likely obstructive HCM; distinguish aortic stenosis.
[R4; Skill E] Request ECG, echo and specialist assessment including arrhythmia/syncope/family history.
[R5; Skill E] Offer first-degree relative screening and individualised exercise advice.
[R6; Skill G] Gain consent, preserve comfort, ask about exertional symptoms.
[G] Gains consent, checks discomfort, and protects dignity during examination.
Fail performance (AMaC educational illustration; not a literal examination outcome).
CANDIDATE: “I will have a quick look.” [R1 Fail]
EXAMINER: “What did you find?”
CANDIDATE: “It is probably hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with family screening and sport.” [R2 Fail; R3 Fail]
EXAMINER: “What happens next?”
CANDIDATE: “I would just follow up routinely.” [R4 Fail; R5 Fail]
Examiner note: The diagnosis is asserted without a supporting sign sequence, an alternative or a safe plan; patient comfort is not established. [R6 Fail]
Pass performance (minimum safe actions performed).
CANDIDATE: “Hello. I would like to examine you to help work out what is going on. Is that okay? Tell me if anything is painful.” [R6 Pass]
CANDIDATE: “Examine pulse, apex, murmur with posture and heart-failure signs. I will do this systematically and help you if you are unsteady.” [R1 Pass]
EXAMINER: “Summarise the key examination findings.”

CANDIDATE: “The patient is comfortable at rest; normal peripheral perfusion and no oedema. A brisk, jerky carotid pulse; double apical impulse; an ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge that increases with standing and decreases with squatting.” [R2 Pass]
EXAMINER: “What is your impression?”
CANDIDATE: “Likely hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with dynamic LV outflow obstruction; echo confirms morphology and gradient. I would also consider relevant alternatives.” [R3 Pass]
EXAMINER: “What would you do next?”
CANDIDATE: “Request ECG, echo and specialist assessment including arrhythmia/syncope/family history. Offer first-degree relative screening and individualised exercise advice.” [R4 Pass; R5 Pass]
Examiner note: Demonstrates a safe, adequately justified assessment and explicit welfare action.
High-performance performance (adds prioritisation and anticipatory reasoning).
CANDIDATE: “Before examining, I will check whether any manoeuvre worsens pain or threatens balance and maintain your privacy.” [R6 High-performance]
CANDIDATE: “Reposition gently; specifically compare standing and squatting effects.” [R1 High-performance]
EXAMINER: “Which signs are discriminating?”
CANDIDATE: “Explain the manoeuvre-related change; do not invent an ejection click. I will state clearly what I did not find.” [R2 High-performance]
EXAMINER: “What else could explain them?”
CANDIDATE: “Also consider hypertensive LVH and other causes of systolic murmurs.” [R3 High-performance]
EXAMINER: “How does that change your plan?”

CANDIDATE: “Discuss CMR, ambulatory ECG and individualised ICD assessment; explain specialist treatment options; reserve mavacamten for nice-eligible cases.” [R4 High-performance; R5 High-performance]
CANDIDATE: “I will document function and arrange appropriate assistance before the patient leaves.” [R6 High-performance]
Examiner note: Uses objective localisation, offers proportionate investigations, anticipates welfare concerns and avoids unjustified certainty.
R1 — Focused cardiac examination: Failing to examine pulse, apex, murmur with posture and heart-failure signs makes the assessment less safe or less discriminating.
R2 — Signs without invention: Failing to describe a jerky pulse, double apex and dynamic systolic murmur makes the assessment less safe or less discriminating.
R3 — Differential and synthesis: Failing to identify likely obstructive HCM; distinguish aortic stenosis makes the assessment less safe or less discriminating.
R4 — Risk and investigations: Failing to request ECG, echo and specialist assessment including arrhythmia/syncope/family history makes the assessment less safe or less discriminating.
“The dynamic murmur makes me consider HCM; I would confirm obstruction on echocardiography.”
“I cannot give a safe sports clearance without an individual risk assessment.”

A dynamic systolic murmur and jerky pulse suggest obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The clinical task is to recognise possible obstruction and discuss risk, family screening and sport without false certainty.

The candidate labels every systolic murmur aortic stenosis, or automatically bans all sport. Pass behaviour is to identify dynamic obstruction and request specialist, individualised exercise and sudden-death risk assessment.
Not a universal ban; specialist shared decision after risk assessment, tailored to symptoms and the sport.
THINK: syncope, arrhythmia and sudden-death risk.
SAY: “This sounds like dynamic outflow obstruction.”
DO: inspect pulse and apex; use posture; arrange echo and specialist review.
NUMBERS: 10-minute examination encounter (AMaC PACES23 guide); NICE TA913 published 2023.
TRAP: automatic disqualification from all sport.
FINISH: risk, family and exercise decisions through specialist shared care.

ESC Guidelines for management of cardiomyopathies (2023) — https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/44/37/3503/7246608 — Supports: HCM assessment, sudden-death evaluation, family and exercise counselling. Access checked 13 October 2026.

NICE TA913 (6 September 2023) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/TA913/chapter/1-Recommendations — Supports: Mavacamten restricted to eligible symptomatic obstructive HCM after optimised treatment. Access checked 13 October 2026.
AHA/ACC HCM guideline (2024) — https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.04.002 — Supports: Shared decisions about sport; avoid blanket prohibition. Access checked 13 October 2026.
